squirrel-removal.intro: Walterboro is the Colleton County seat and the front porch of the Lowcountry — a historic town of older homes under live oaks and pines, standing at the edge of the ACE Basin's great swamp system. Its squirrels are swamp-stocked: gray squirrels in the town canopy in numbers the inland towns do not match, fed by oak mast and bordered by bottomless woods on the town's wet side. They den in the attics of Walterboro's pre-war and Victorian-era homes, chew in at the eaves under the moss-draped limbs, and treat the historic district's layered rooflines as a connected burrow system above the streets. A Walterboro roof is never the only roof a colony is using; it is the one you own.
squirrel-removal.extendedBody:
Swamp-edge colonies and connected rooflines

Walterboro's exclusions are planned as street-level work. The canopy over the historic district is continuous, the rooflines touch it everywhere, and a colony excluded from one house tests the adjacent roofs the same week — so we seal your house as a building inside a connected system: every entry found, not just the active one, rebuilt in metal; the chimney capped; the limb bridges to your roof mapped for trimming. The surrounding swamp guarantees the pressure is permanent, which is precisely why the seal has to be complete — in ACE Basin country, a partial seal is a brief vacancy. Bats share these attics in summer and are read for in the same inspection, as are the flying squirrels that work the swamp-edge oaks at night. One visit, the whole roof's tenant list, and a sealing programme priced once.

faqs.q: How much does squirrel removal cost in Walterboro?
faqs.a: It depends on the roofline — Walterboro's older homes carry the layered junctions that take time to map, and the seal has to cover all of them to hold in swamp country. We inspect the full perimeter and the canopy over it, quote the complete job firmly, and include the check for the attic's other tenants in the same visit. In a town where the woods restock every roof, the complete seal is not the premium option; it is the only version that is not rented.

faqs.q: Our Walterboro home is in the historic district. Will the sealing show?
faqs.a: It is specified not to. Entries are rebuilt in metal fitted and finished to sit quietly against old trim, screens are matched to the existing vent patterns, and chimney caps are chosen for brick that has stood a century. The junctions we seal are also the junctions that leak weather, so the work reads as maintenance — because it is maintenance, done from the animal side. We photograph every seal for your records, which in the historic district doubles as documentation of the home's upkeep.

mole-removal.intro: Lodge is a Colleton County crossroads in the Lowcountry's flatwoods — a small rural community of farms and older homes between Walterboro and the Edisto country, on deep sandy soil threaded by swamp branches. Its moles are the sand's moles: eastern moles tunnelling the yards, gardens, and church grounds in systems that surface overnight, following the earthworm lines that the moist Lowcountry topsoil keeps near the surface most of the year. In a community Lodge's size the mole work is personal-scale — a garden being rooted nightly, a yard gone soft along the runs, a well-kept lawn losing an argument with the soil it stands on — and the answer is the same unglamorous one: the active system, trapped properly, over the weeks a campaign takes.
mole-removal.extendedBody:
Crossroads ground, campaign method

Lodge mole work starts by separating the working tunnels from last month's. In sand, runs collapse and re-form constantly, so we press the surface lines and return to read which have re-inflated — those are the feeding runs in use — and we find the deep highways along the foundations, the drive edges, and the old fence lines where the system travels. Sets go on the active ground and are worked on a checking cycle until the yard reads quiet, and the whole programme is quoted as one price at the survey, because rural work runs on trust and a per-visit meter destroys it. The garden conversation matters here: Lodge's gardens are a point of pride and a grub-and-worm pantry, and we will say plainly if the beds are feeding the system — the fix is rarely to stop gardening; it is to trap the system out and treat the grub load where it is heaviest, so the garden stops advertising itself to every dispersing mole in the flatwoods.

faqs.q: How much does mole removal cost in Lodge?
faqs.a: It depends on the ground — most Lodge properties are a standard campaign on a single active system; a large farmhouse lot with garden and foundation runs is longer. We survey first, mark what is active, and quote the full programme as one firm price covering the sets and the scheduled checks until the ground is quiet. We are glad to quote it at the kitchen table with the survey in hand, which in a community this size is how the number should be delivered.

faqs.q: Moles are rooting our Lodge garden every night. Will trapping the yard save it?
faqs.a: Trapping the active system is what saves it — the rooting is one or two residents working the beds for grubs and worms, and removing them stops the nightly damage outright. What we add is the grub assessment: a bed heavy with grubs is re-let quickly once vacant, because the flatwoods around Lodge keep producing young moles looking for exactly that pantry. Trapping plus the grub conversation is the durable version; trapping alone, in a stocked garden, is a season's truce — and we will tell you which one your garden needs before you pay for either.
